title: Wave intensity, power and area
prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy without a net transfer of matter.
Power is the rate of energy transfer and is measured in watts.
From Lesson 6, wave graphs represent measured displacement rather than the route travelled by energy.
new_learning: Use intensity as power transferred per unit area.
Distinguish source power from intensity at a location.
Use supplied geometry to find the area over which wave power is spread.
not_yet_taught: Use intensity proportional to amplitude squared.
Infer an amplitude change from an intensity change.

blocks.heading: The same loudspeaker, two different readings
content: A loudspeaker sends out steady wave power. One small detector is close to it and another is far away. The source has not changed, so why can the distant detector receive less power?
The missing idea is how widely the transferred power is spread at the detector's location. We need a quantity that combines power and area.

figure.purpose: Create the need to distinguish fixed source power from local intensity.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of one wave source with a near and far detector. Draw the same outward energy flow spreading through a narrow near arc and wider far arc. Label only source power fixed and area larger farther away.
figure.alt_text: One source sends wave power across a larger area at a farther detector.

blocks.heading: Intensity measures how concentrated the power is
content: Wave intensity tells us how much wave power passes through each unit area. A high intensity means the transferred power is concentrated. A low intensity means it is spread more thinly.

The formula to remember is $I = \frac{P}{A}$. Here $I$ is wave intensity in watts per square metre, W m$^{-2}$; $P$ is power transferred by the wave in watts, W; and $A$ is area normal to the direction of energy transfer in square metres, m$^2$.

The area must face the energy flow. If a detector is tilted, its surface area is not automatically the area normal to the wave direction. In this lesson, any needed normal area is given or follows directly from the supplied geometry.

figure.purpose: Make power per normal area and the units visible.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper sketch of parallel wave-energy arrows crossing a square frame at right angles. Annotate power P crossing normal area A, then show I=P/A and units W divided by m squared equals W m to the minus two.
figure.alt_text: Wave power crosses an area normal to energy transfer, giving intensity P divided by A.

blocks.heading: A beam with a known cross-section
content: A wave beam transfers 18 W uniformly through a cross-sectional area of 0.060 m$^2$. The area is already normal to the beam, so use it directly.

A unit check gives W divided by m$^2$, exactly the unit of intensity. A scale check also works: the power crosses much less than one square metre, so the numerical intensity should be greater than 18 W m$^{-2}$.

figure.purpose: Model a complete direct intensity calculation with units and an independent scale check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout beside a simple beam cross-section. Use boxes for known P=18 W, A=0.060 m squared, formula, substitution, result 300 W m to the minus two, and a small unit-and-scale check.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout finds 300 watts per square metre from 18 watts over 0.060 square metre.

blocks.heading: Source power and local intensity are not the same
content: Power describes the total rate at which the wave transfers energy. Intensity describes that power per unit area at a chosen location. Their units are different because they answer different questions.

Imagine the same 12 W shared equally across four 1 m$^2$ tiles. Each tile receives 3 W, so the intensity is 3 W m$^{-2}$. If the same 12 W is shared across twelve such tiles, the intensity is 1 W m$^{-2}$. The source power stayed 12 W while the local intensity changed.
This distinction is why a detector reading can fall even when the source keeps transferring energy at the same rate.

figure.purpose: Contrast fixed total power with two different areas and intensities.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table. Left: 12 W distributed over four equal tiles, 3 W on each. Right: 12 W over twelve equal tiles, 1 W on each. Highlight same total power and different power per tile.
figure.alt_text: Twelve watts spread over four tiles is more intense than twelve watts spread over twelve tiles.

blocks.heading: When the geometry supplies a spherical area
content: Suppose a small source transfers 25 W uniformly through a complete spherical surface of radius 2.0 m. The geometry supplies the spreading area: $A = 4\pi r^2$.
$A = 4\pi(2.0)^2 = 50.3$ m$^2$. Then $I = \frac{25}{50.3} = 0.497$ W m$^{-2}$, which is 0.50 W m$^{-2}$ to two significant figures.
Check the result another way. The 25 W is spread over about 50 m$^2$, so about 0.5 W passes through each square metre. This agrees with the calculation.
We used the spherical area because the question supplied uniform spreading over a complete sphere. We do not assume a spherical model when the geometry is not given.

figure.purpose: Connect supplied spherical geometry to a two-stage area-then-intensity calculation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-stage sketch. Show a point source at the centre of a sphere with radius 2.0 m, then a calculation flow from A=4 pi r squared to 50.3 m squared and I=25/50.3 to 0.50 W m to the minus two.
figure.alt_text: A source spreads 25 watts uniformly over a sphere of radius 2.0 metres.

blocks.heading: Lower intensity does not mean energy vanished
content: It feels reasonable to say that lower intensity means the wave has lost power. That can happen in an absorbing medium, but spreading alone does not prove it.
If the same power crosses a larger supplied area, each square metre receives a smaller share. The local intensity falls even while the total power crossing the complete area remains the same.
Always separate the two questions: what is the total power, and over what normal area is that power distributed? Only then calculate intensity.

figure.purpose: Correct the belief that every decrease in local intensity proves a loss of total power.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper misconception panel with two concentric supplied surfaces. Show the same count of energy markers crossing each complete surface but fewer markers per equal patch on the larger surface. Add the cue same total, smaller share per square metre.
figure.alt_text: The same total wave power is less concentrated on a larger surface.

blocks.heading: A reliable intensity routine
content: First identify the wave power that crosses the surface. Do not confuse it with energy or with an intensity reading.
Second identify the area normal to energy transfer. Use the supplied cross-section or calculate the area from geometry that the question explicitly gives.
Third use $I = P/A$, carry units through the substitution, and report W m$^{-2}$.
Finally check meaning. A fixed power spread over a larger area should give a smaller intensity. This lesson does not connect intensity to amplitude; that relationship comes next.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the power-area-intensity method and its scope boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map with boxes: identify P, find normal A from supplied geometry, calculate I=P/A, check units and concentration. End with a stop sign labelled no amplitude relationship yet.
figure.alt_text: A four-step routine calculates and checks wave intensity without using amplitude.
